items.followUp: What is hydrogen bonding? Name one substance in which it occurs.

rubric.why: Checks that the answer identifies the kind of intermolecular attraction involved in hydrogen bonding.
rubric.description: Identifies hydrogen bonding as an attraction involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as F, O or N.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the attraction between hydrogen and an electronegative atom (usually F, O or N), especially between molecules.

rubric.why: Checks for a correct example of a substance whose molecules can form hydrogen bonds.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as water, hydrogen fluoride or ammonia.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and an electronegative atom of another molecule.

items.followUp: State the three ways atoms can achieve a stable outer electron shell.

rubric.why: Checks for all three ways atoms can achieve an octet; each way is needed for a complete answer.
rubric.description: States that atoms can lose, gain or share electrons to accommodate eight electrons in the valence shell.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for all three ways; award 1 mark if only two are stated.

modelAnswer: An atom can accommodate eight electrons in its valence shell by losing electrons, gaining electrons or sharing electrons.

rubric.why: Checks the state change that defines melting point.
rubric.description: Defines melting point as the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct solid-to-liquid change.

rubric.why: Checks the state change that defines boiling point.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point as the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct liquid-to-gas change.

modelAnswer: Melting point is the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid.
Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas.

items.followUp: Define crystalline solids and give one example.

rubric.why: Checks the defining arrangement of particles in an amorphous solid.
rubric.description: States that amorphous solids have particles arranged irregularly, without a regular pattern.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the irregular arrangement of particles.

rubric.why: Checks that the student can give a valid example.
rubric.description: Gives one example, such as glass, plastic or rubber.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: Amorphous solids are solids whose particles are not arranged in a regular pattern.
Glass is an example of an amorphous solid.

items.followUp: Write the atomic number and electronic configuration of sodium.

rubric.why: Checks the factual atomic number of chlorine.
rubric.description: States that chlorine has atomic number 17.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct atomic number.

rubric.why: Checks the distribution of chlorine's electrons among shells or orbitals.
rubric.description: Gives chlorine's electronic configuration as 2, 8, 7 (or the equivalent orbital configuration).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct configuration.

items.followUp: How does ionization energy change as electropositivity increases?

accept: as electropositivity increases ionization energy decreases
rubric.why: Checks the direction of the relationship between the two properties.
rubric.description: States that electropositivity and ionization energy are inversely related.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the inverse relationship.

rubric.why: Checks the chemical explanation for the inverse relationship.
rubric.description: Explains that electropositive atoms lose electrons more readily, so less energy is needed to remove an electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct explanation.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity and ionization energy are inversely related.
An electropositive atom loses an electron readily, so its ionization energy is low.

items.followUp: Explain why water dissolves many ionic compounds, and give one example.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of the principle that like substances dissolve like substances.
rubric.description: States that polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct principle.

rubric.why: Checks that the principle is illustrated with a valid solute-solvent pair.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example, such as sodium chloride in water or iodine in carbon tetrachloride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that polar substances dissolve in polar solvents, while non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.
For example, sodium chloride dissolves in water.

items.followUp: What does a 3% V/m solution indicate?

rubric.why: Checks that the student identifies the volume of solute used in the percentage.
rubric.description: Explains that V/m percentage compares the volume of solute with the mass of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying volume of solute relative to mass of solution.

rubric.why: Checks the standard per-100-g basis and/or a valid numerical illustration of V/m percentage.
rubric.description: States the amount as volume of solute in 100 g of solution, with a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the per-100-g basis and giving a consistent example.

modelAnswer: V/m percentage is the volume of solute, in cm³, present in 100 g of solution.
For example, a 5% V/m solution contains 5 cm³ of solute in 100 g of solution.
